headline: Kennebec Stripers Working Mackerel Schools, Monhegan Ledges Holding Pollock and a Few Cod
subhead: River bass are feeding steady in daylight while the Gulf keeps its cool, and the ledges off Monhegan are still worth the run for groundfish.
body_markdown:
Forty-some years ago an old lobsterman named Elden Poole told me the Kennebec doesn't care what the calendar says, it cares what the water's doing underneath it. I was twenty-two and thought that was just old-man talk. Took me another decade to understand he meant the current, not the tide chart, and by the time I did I'd already learned it the hard way — anchored up off Doubling Point on a slack tide with nothing to show for it while the fish were stacked two hundred yards downriver on a seam I hadn't bothered to find. I think about Elden every July when the mackerel push into the rivers and the bass follow them in, because that lesson hasn't gotten any less true.

That's exactly what's happening right now from the Kennebec down through the Sheepscot and into the Damariscotta. Striped bass are holding on the outgoing tide around Fort Popham, the Bath waterfront, and the narrows above Damariscotta village, feeding hard on schools of mackerel that have been thick as smoke this month. Unlike what's happening south of the Cape, where the bass have gone nocturnal to dodge warm water, our fish up here are still eating in daylight — the Gulf of Maine keeps its influence strong enough that the rivers never get uncomfortable for them, even in mid-July. I've had good mornings drifting live mackerel on a fish-finder rig, 3/0 circle hook, just enough weight to hold bottom in eight to twelve feet on the last two hours of the ebb. Topwater has worked too — a white Slug-Go worked slow over the grass flats at first light has drawn some good strikes, fish running 28 to 34 inches, with the occasional overslot mixed in around the deeper holes below the Route 1 bridge in Wiscasset.

The mackerel themselves are worth mentioning on their own account. Boothbay Harbor and the water off Ocean Point have had them stacked tight enough that a Sabiki rig with six hooks will load up in under a minute most mornings on the last of the incoming. Good for the smoker, good for bait, and honestly good sport on light spinning gear if you're not in a hurry to go anywhere else.

Offshore, the groundfish pattern is holding steady but it remains cold-water dependent, same as it's been the last few Julys. Monhegan's ledges — the water off Manana and out toward the southeast corner — are giving up pollock that are schooling right on the surface some mornings, chasing bait up where you can see them roll. Jigging diamond jigs or Hopkins spoons through that surface activity has been productive, fish in the 8 to 15 pound range, some bigger. Cod are still there too, but they've dropped down onto the deeper ledges, 120 to 170 feet, and you need to work bottom with a jig or a bait rig tipped with clam to connect. It's not the volume fishing it was thirty years ago — nobody up here pretends otherwise — but a few decent cod a trip is a realistic expectation if you're willing to work the drift right.

Penobscot Bay itself has been a mixed bag. The channel between Islesboro and the mainland, and the deeper water off Vinalhaven toward the Fox Island Thorofare, are holding some groundfish in that 90 to 130 foot range, but it's spotty — some drifts you'll mark fish stacked on the sounder and get nothing, others you'll pick at a couple pollock and call it good. Haddock have thinned out closer in and pushed farther toward Matinicus, which tracks with what usually happens by mid-July. If you're running that far, it's worth the extra hour, but I wouldn't plan a whole trip around it without a backup.

Bluefish haven't shown in any real numbers up this way yet, and with the bunker schools mostly holding south of the Cape right now, I don't expect that to change fast. If that bait keeps pushing north the way it's been talked about all month, there's a chance we see a few blues nose into the outer bay by early August, but that's speculation on my part, not something I'm seeing on the water yet.

With the moon working toward first quarter on the 21st, current strength will ease up through the week, which usually means slower presentations produce better than fast ones — good news for the mackerel-and-bait crowd in the rivers, less good for anyone relying on a hard rip to concentrate fish out on the ledges. My plan for the coming week is simple: mornings in the Kennebec and Damariscotta on the last of the ebb while the bass are still willing to eat in daylight, and if the wind lays down out of the south like it's been forecast, a run out to Monhegan to see if those pollock are still showing on top. If the wind doesn't cooperate, Penobscot Bay's channels are close enough to fish anyway, even if the numbers are thinner than out at the island.
